blocks.explain: The header is written by the client, and the name is chosen by the client. Check the content, generate the name, and store outside the web root so even a file that slips through can never run.

blocks.question: Why does OWASP say to apply the size limit after decompression for archives?
options: Compressed files are always safe
Decompression changes the file signature
Archives cannot contain executable files
A small compressed file can expand to an enormous size (a zip bomb) and fill disk or memory when the server unpacks it
blocks.explain: Compression ratios can be extreme, so a few kilobytes can become gigabytes. Limit the expanded size, using safe extraction code that counts bytes as it goes.

lessons.title: When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon

blocks.md:
Most sites put a **front end** (a load balancer, CDN (content delivery network) or reverse proxy: a server that receives requests on behalf of others) in front of **back-end** application servers. For speed, the front end sends many users' requests one after another over the same reused back-end connection. Each server must work out where one request ends and the next begins.

HTTP/1.1 has two ways to say how long a request body is. **Content-Length** gives the size in bytes. **Transfer-Encoding: chunked** sends the body in pieces, each prefixed with its size in hexadecimal, ending with a zero-size chunk. If a request carries both and the two servers believe different headers, they disagree about the boundary. The leftover bytes are then read by the back end as the **start of the next request**, which may belong to another user. That is **HTTP request smuggling**: the attacker smuggles a partial request inside their own.

blocks.title: One connection, two different readings

scenes.caption: Simplified model: one reused connection carries the attacker's request A, then a victim's request B. Cells are pieces of bytes, not real syntax.
The front end trusts one length header and reads A as header, body and an extra piece X. It forwards all three, then later forwards B.
The back end trusts the other length header. For it, A ends after the body. X is left in the buffer, waiting.
When B arrives, the back end reads X followed by B's header as one request. The victim's request now begins with bytes the attacker chose.

blocks.md:
Consequences, from PortSwigger: bypassing front-end security controls (the front end checked A, not X), capturing other users' requests, and poisoning caches. The technique was first documented in 2005 by researchers at Watchfire, a web security company, and revived in 2019 by James Kettle, director of research at PortSwigger, in *HTTP Desync Attacks*.

**Defences.** [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html), the HTTP/1.1 standard, says a server MAY reject a request with both headers or use Transfer-Encoding alone, and MUST close the connection after responding to such a request. In practice: make the front end **normalise or reject** ambiguous requests, use **HTTP/2 end to end** (its framing has one length mechanism, so PortSwigger notes it is immune to this ambiguity, though downgrading HTTP/2 to HTTP/1 at the front end reintroduces it), or stop reusing back-end connections, at a performance cost.

**Case: ProxyLogon, 2021.** Microsoft Exchange, the email server many organisations run themselves, is split into a front-end proxy and back-end services, and the front end authenticates to the back end with Kerberos (a ticket-based network login protocol from MIT, named after the three-headed dog that guards Hades) **as the Exchange server itself**. Orange Tsai of DEVCORE found that this proxy could be pointed at the wrong place; DEVCORE named the bug after Exchange's *Proxy* architecture and *Logon* mechanism.

Google Project Zero's (a Google bug-hunting team) root-cause analysis of CVE-2021-26855: requests for static-looking resources were routed to a back-end server named in a **cookie**, and the URL builder joined that value by plain string concatenation. So an unauthenticated request could make the front end call **any back-end endpoint, with the server's own credentials**: SSRF and a confused deputy at once. Chained with CVE-2021-27065, an arbitrary file write available after authentication, it gave code execution through port 443 alone.

blocks.title: ProxyLogon at the level of ideas

scenes.caption: The attacker sends an unauthenticated request for what looks like a static file, with a routing cookie whose value names a back-end endpoint.
The front end builds the back-end URL from the cookie by string concatenation and forwards the request, authenticated as the Exchange server.
The back end trusts the front end's identity, so the attacker can act with administrator-level access: an authentication bypass.
The second bug, a post-authentication arbitrary file write, is used to place a web shell in a directory the server executes.
From then on the attacker runs commands through the web shell. Patching later does not remove it, which is why responders hunted for web shells.

blocks.md:
**What happened.** [Volexity](https://www.volexity.com/blog/2021/03/02/active-exploitation-of-microsoft-exchange-zero-day-vulnerabilities/), a security firm, saw exploitation from early January 2021, noticed because its network monitoring showed a large amount of data being sent from two customers' Exchange servers to unknown IP addresses: an egress signal. Microsoft released fixes in early March 2021. Brian Krebs reported that at least 30,000 US organisations were hacked in the days that followed, and CISA's [Emergency Directive 21-02](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-21-02-mitigate-microsoft-exchange-premises-product-vulnerabilities) required federal agencies to forensically triage and patch their Exchange servers.

The pattern across this lesson: **two components that parse or trust the same request differently**. Smuggling is a disagreement about where a request ends; ProxyLogon is a front end trusting a value the user supplied and a back end trusting the front end. Fix by making each component validate what it receives, not what it assumes the other checked.

Whenever one server forwards to another, ask two questions: do both agree on what the request *is* (its boundaries, its host, its path), and does the back end trust the front end's identity for actions the original user was never allowed to do?

blocks.question: Which architecture change removes the classic Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding ambiguity?
options: Adding a second HTTP/1.1 proxy
Increasing the Content-Length limit
Speaking HTTP/2 from the client all the way to the back end
Turning on gzip compression
blocks.explain: HTTP/2 frames carry their own lengths, so there is one way to find a request's end. A front end that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 for the back end brings the ambiguity back, which is where newer variants live.

blocks.question: In ProxyLogon, why did the back end perform privileged actions for an unauthenticated attacker?
options: The attacker cracked an admin password
Exchange had no back end
The front end forwarded the attacker-routed request using the Exchange server's own Kerberos identity, which the back end trusted
The attacker used request smuggling
blocks.explain: The front end lent its own credentials to a request whose destination the attacker chose: SSRF with a confused deputy. The fix validated the routing value as a host name and stopped the front end from authenticating such requests as itself.

lessons.title: Detecting server-side attacks and the defence map

blocks.md: Every attack in this course makes the server do something it normally never does: connect somewhere new, read a file outside its directory, load a class it never uses, write a script into its web root, or call a cloud API from an unusual place. Detection means collecting the logs where those actions show up and knowing which signal each attack produces. Prevention means taking the choice away from input and shrinking what the server can touch.

blocks.title: Which log lights up for which attack

nodes.label:
Host / EDR: processes
and file writes

scenes.caption: The log sources. Front-door logs see the attacker's request; the others see what the server did because of it.
SSRF to cloud metadata: odd URL parameters at the WAF, egress denials, IMDS metric changes, then CloudTrail calls with the role's keys from a new IP.
XXE: DOCTYPE in request bodies at the WAF, entity or DTD errors in app logs, and outbound fetches from the XML service.
Log4Shell: lookup syntax in headers, outbound LDAP and odd DNS names from Java servers, and the Java process spawning shells.
Deserialization, uploads, Spring4Shell, ProxyLogon: new script files in web directories and unusual child processes on the host.
Path traversal: ../ and encoded dots in requests, 200 responses for files outside the app, and reads of unusual files by the web process.

blocks.md:
**The defence map**, one line per bug class:

- **SSRF**: no full URLs from users; allowlist and resolved-IP checks; no redirects; isolated fetchers; default-deny egress; IMDSv2 with hop limit 1; least-privilege roles.
- **XXE**: disable DTDs in every XML parser (one shared factory); defusedxml in Python; restrict formats that hide XML.
- **Deserialization**: JSON plus schema; never native formats from users; class allowlist filters and HMAC signing if unavoidable.
- **Lookups and expression languages (Log4Shell, OGNL, binding)**: patch fast with an SBOM; never evaluate user text; binding allowlists; egress filtering as the safety net.
- **Path traversal**: IDs not names; normalise then compare whole components.
- **Uploads**: check bytes, rename, store outside the web root, scan, limit size.
- **Smuggling and proxy trust**: reject ambiguous requests; HTTP/2 end to end; back ends validate, not assume.

The two controls that appear in almost every row: **egress filtering** (it breaks the SSRF, XXE and Log4Shell chains at the network) and **least privilege** for the server's own identity (it would have bounded Capital One's role, the databases Equifax's stolen credentials reached and every web shell). Both work against bugs you have not found yet.

blocks.prompt: Your web app's egress proxy logs a denied connection from the Java order service to an unknown host on port 389 at 03:12, and nothing else looks wrong. What is your first hypothesis and your next two checks?
blocks.reveal:
Port 389 is LDAP, and a Java service reaching out to an unknown LDAP server is the classic Log4Shell callback (or another JNDI injection). Next checks:

1. **What was logged just before 03:12** by that service and the systems that feed it: search for lookup syntax in headers, form fields and stored data passed along to it.
2. **Which Log4j versions are inside that service**, including transitive dependencies (dependency tree, SBOM, or the jar search from lesson 10).

The denial means the chain probably broke at the network, but upgrade anyway and check for other outbound attempts that were allowed.

blocks.md:
**Practice, legally.** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Free, legal labs that match this course:

- PortSwigger Web Security Academy: [SSRF](https://portswigger.net/web-security/ssrf), [XXE](https://portswigger.net/web-security/xxe), [insecure deserialization](https://portswigger.net/web-security/deserialization), [path traversal](https://portswigger.net/web-security/file-path-traversal), [file upload](https://portswigger.net/web-security/file-upload) and [request smuggling](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling).
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/), a deliberately insecure shop app with challenges that include XXE and upload flaws.
- On your own machine, the harmless demos in this course: the Log4j 2.14.1 versus 2.17.1 lookup test, the JDK XXE test and the pickle stack trace, all with placeholder data.

blocks.question: A team can do only one thing this quarter. Which control reduces the impact of the widest range of server-side attacks, including ones not yet discovered?
options: Default-deny egress from application servers, with an allowlist and logging
A WAF rule for each new CVE
Renaming admin URLs
Disabling HTTP/2
blocks.explain: Egress control breaks SSRF to internal hosts, XXE and Log4Shell callbacks and many exfiltration paths, and its denials are evidence. WAF rules lag behind each new variant; renaming URLs is obscurity, not control.

blocks.question: CloudTrail shows the EC2 role of your image-resizing service listing S3 buckets from an IP address outside AWS. What does this most likely mean?
options: Normal behaviour for resizing images
CloudTrail is misconfigured
The bucket is public
The instance's temporary credentials were stolen, for example via SSRF to the metadata service, and are being used elsewhere
blocks.explain: Instance role credentials should only be used from the instance. Use from an external IP is what GuardDuty's InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding flags. Revoke the role's sessions, find the SSRF, and check what was read.
